title: How to Know If Your AC Is Low on Refrigerant
h1: How Do You Know If Your AC Is Low on Refrigerant?
description: The signs your AC is low on refrigerant, why it means there is a leak, what you can safely check yourself, and why refrigerant work is a job for a technician.
quick_answer: Common signs your AC is low on refrigerant include warm or barely cool air from the vents, ice on the indoor coil or the copper line outside, a hissing or bubbling sound, and an AC that runs constantly without reaching the set temperature. Refrigerant doesn't get used up, so low refrigerant means a leak that a technician needs to find and repair.
body:
What are the signs of low refrigerant?

Low refrigerant shows up in a few ways. You may notice one or several of these:

  • Air from the vents isn't very cold, even though the system is running.
  • The AC runs much longer than usual and the house never quite reaches the thermostat setting.
  • Ice or frost on the larger copper line at the outdoor unit or on the indoor coil.
  • Hissing or bubbling sounds near the indoor or outdoor unit, which can point to a leak.
  • Higher electric bills with no change in how you use the AC.
  • Water around the indoor unit after ice on the coil melts.

None of these signs alone proves the refrigerant is low. A dirty filter, a dirty coil or a weak blower can cause some of the same symptoms. That's why a technician checks the whole system.

Does an AC use up refrigerant over time?

No. Refrigerant circulates in a sealed loop and isn't consumed like gas in a car. If the level is low, the refrigerant went somewhere, which means there's a leak.

That's why simply topping it off isn't a real fix. The system will lose the new charge too, sometimes over weeks and sometimes over a season. A proper repair finds the leak, fixes it, then charges the system to the manufacturer's specification.

What can you safely check yourself?

You can rule out a few common look-alikes before calling:

  1. Check the filter. A clogged filter restricts airflow and can make the coil freeze. Replace it if it's dirty.
  2. Check the thermostat. Make sure it's on cool, set below room temperature and the fan is on auto.
  3. Look at the outdoor unit. Make sure it's running and the coil isn't blocked by plants, leaves or stored items. Keep a couple of feet of clearance around it.
  4. Check supply vents and returns. Make sure they're open and not blocked by furniture.

If you see ice on the coil or lines, turn the AC off and set the fan to on so the ice can melt. Running a frozen system can damage the compressor.

Why shouldn't you add refrigerant yourself?

Refrigerant work requires EPA certification, the right gauges and recovery equipment, and knowledge of the specific refrigerant your system uses. DIY recharge kits can overcharge the system, introduce the wrong refrigerant or sealants, and damage the compressor. They also do nothing about the leak.

Refrigerant can cause frostbite on contact, and the system runs at high pressure. This is a job for a technician.

Where do AC refrigerant leaks usually happen?

Leaks tend to show up at a few spots:

  • The indoor coil, where small pinhole leaks can develop over time
  • Brazed joints and flare fittings at the line set
  • Service valves on the outdoor unit
  • The outdoor coil, especially in coastal neighborhoods where salt air speeds up corrosion
  • Places where copper lines rub against a wall, fence or each other

A technician uses electronic leak detectors, bubble solution or other tests to pinpoint the leak. Depending on where it is, the fix may be a repair, a replacement part like the indoor coil, or, for an older system with an obsolete refrigerant, a conversation about replacement.

What does a technician check?

A refrigerant diagnosis is more than hooking up gauges. A technician will usually check the filter, blower and coils first, since airflow problems can look like a low charge. Then they measure pressures and temperatures at the system to compare against the manufacturer's targets. If the numbers point to a low charge, the next step is finding the leak before any refrigerant is added.

What happens if you keep running an AC that's low on refrigerant?

It gets more expensive the longer it goes. The system runs longer to cool less, so energy use goes up. The compressor can overheat because refrigerant also helps cool it. Coils can freeze and drip water. Eventually, the compressor can fail, which is one of the most costly repairs on an AC.

If you notice the signs above, especially during a hot inland summer when the system works hardest, have it checked soon. Our AC repair technicians can diagnose the issue, find the leak and tell you your options.
faqs: How often should AC refrigerant be recharged?

Ideally never. A properly installed, leak-free system keeps the same refrigerant charge for its whole life. If your AC needs refrigerant added regularly, it has a leak that should be found and repaired.
Why is there ice on my AC lines?

Ice on the refrigerant lines or indoor coil usually means low airflow or low refrigerant. Check the filter first. Then turn the AC off and run the fan to melt the ice, and call for service if it happens again or the filter was clean.
Can low refrigerant damage my AC?

Yes. Running with low refrigerant makes the compressor work harder and run hotter, can freeze the coil and can eventually cause the compressor to fail. Catching a leak early is much less costly than replacing a compressor.
My AC is old. Is it worth fixing a refrigerant leak?

It depends on the age of the system, where the leak is and what refrigerant it uses. Older systems that use phased-out refrigerant can be costly to recharge. A technician can lay out repair and replacement options so you can decide.
How Do You Recharge an AC System, and Should You Do It Yourself?

A home AC system shouldn't need a recharge unless it has a leak, since refrigerant isn't used up over time. The right fix is finding and repairing the leak, then charging the system to the manufacturer's specifications. Handling refrigerant takes certified technicians and specialized gauges, so this isn't a do-it-yourself job.
